html:
The Roman Republic was the state ruled from the city of Rome between the expulsion of its last king, traditionally in 509 BCE, and the rise of Augustus as sole ruler in 27 BCE. In those five centuries Rome grew from one town in central Italy to the master of the Mediterranean.

Power was shared out so that no one person held it for long. Two consuls were elected each year, the Senate of former officials gave advice that was rarely refused, and assemblies of citizens voted on laws and elections. Early struggles between patricians and plebeians produced written law, the Twelve Tables, in about 450 BCE.

How it grew:

  • Conquest of Italy by about 270 BCE, through wars and a web of allies.
  • Victory over Carthage in the First and Second Punic Wars, which gave Rome Sicily, Spain and the western sea.
  • Wars in the Greek east, ending Macedon in 168 BCE; Carthage and Corinth were both destroyed in 146 BCE.

Empire brought slaves, loot and huge estates, while small farmers who served in the army lost out. The reforms of Tiberius Gracchus in 133 BCE ended in his murder, and politics turned violent. Generals such as Marius and Sulla used armies loyal to themselves to win power at home. Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, won a civil war and was killed in 44 BCE. His heir Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE and became Augustus, the first emperor of the Roman Empire. The forms of the Republic survived; its substance did not.
